rows.claim: fp16 grad scaler skips an overflowing step
rows.control_arm: inject an overflow; scaler must SKIP, loss must not become nan
rows.status: MEASURED and GREEN on a GB200 tray, with a control that could have fired and did. History: this row read "never run". The first thing the adjudicator had to settle is what the row is even about, because FoundationScale constructs no grad scaler anywhere -- a grep for GradScaler over src/foundationscale returns nothing. What it does instead is declare precision by setting the fp16 flag on a transformers TrainingArguments inside train/loop.py, after which transformers and accelerate own the scaler. So this row is a claim about the composed system, and the adjudicator says so in its own docstring rather than pretending the framework implements the skip itself. It runs three things. A declaration pin parses the installed foundationscale.train.loop with ast -- located through importlib find_spec, so it pins the package that would actually run rather than a file that happens to sit near it on disk -- and asserts the mapping from precision fp16 onto the fp16 flag is still there; without it the row would stay green while measuring only transformers, which is the failure mode of every test that reproduces a literal instead of exercising a code path. The pin is controlled both ways before being trusted: against the real source it reports the mapping present, and against a shadowed package whose mapping has been deleted it reports it absent, because a pin that cannot fire is decoration. A wiring arm then builds that declaration, drives a Trainer to the point where accelerate materialises its scaler, and resolves the live object instead of hand-building one. Finally two behavioural arms run the identical sequence through that one live scaler with the injected gradient as the only difference between them, so a divergence in their outcomes is attributable to the overflow and to nothing else. Measured on the tray: the scaler resolved at trainer.accelerator.scaler as a torch.amp.grad_scaler.GradScaler, enabled, at an initial scale of 65536. The run arm's finite gradient of 0.5 was scaled to 32768.0, unscaled back to exactly 0.5, and the parameter moved 1.0 to 0.5, so the step was taken and the scale was left alone. The control arm's infinite gradient survived as inf through both scale and unscale, the parameter stayed at exactly 1.0, the step was skipped, the scale was halved to 32768.0, and nothing became nan. The comparison is exact equality rather than a tolerance because whether the optimizer stepped is a discrete question, and a tolerance would only make room for a shrunken write to be scored as a skip. The verdict order refuses before it judges: 95 if the framework's loop module is not locatable here at all, because then its behaviour is absent rather than wrong; 5 if it IS locatable and no longer makes the declaration, because nothing downstream can skip an overflowing step and the claim fails upstream of the scaler; 96 if no scaler object resolves, since that is an instrument that cannot find what it tests; 96 if the two arms did not start from the same parameter value, since that is two instruments rather than one run twice; then 5 for a declaration that produced a disabled scaler, 5 for a control that did not skip, 5 for a run arm that DID skip -- a scaler that skips everything would pass the control while being useless, so both directions are required -- 5 for nan, and 0. The self-test drives that pure verdict function over synthetic payloads with no torch, no GPU, no network and no filesystem, and passes 17 of 17 controls, with a MUST-FIRE for every branch above and four that pin the ORDER, including one asserting that a missing framework outranks a missing scaler and one asserting that a dropped declaration is reported as the declaration failure rather than as the control failure it also causes. Honest limitation, stated rather than buried: this measures the handoff, not a skip inside a live training step. It establishes that the declaration is still made, that the declaration buys an enabled scaler, and that the scaler behaves correctly in both directions when handed an overflow. Watching the skip happen inside a real forward and backward over a 7.94B-parameter checkpoint is a separate and far more expensive reading, and this row does not yet carry it.

rows.claim: a 4-bit (nvfp4) declaration REFUSES, never falls back to bf16

rows.status: MEASURED GREEN on a tray at 1460560 (#478), adjudicated by t1_3_nvfp4_refusal_arms.py, whose twenty-one self-test controls pin the verdict order. Taken twice: once against the estate's working checkout and once against a pristine clone of main at 55a1bb6 with a clean worktree, because the working checkout carries an uncommitted local patch and a number published from a modified tree is not a number about this repository. Both takes agree arm for arm. This row previously asserted its refusal with no adjudicator and was the last one doing so. Exit codes alone could not have settled it: this plane reaches 96 from two independent channels -- the config validator rejecting a precision outside PRECISIONS, and the training loop refusing nvfp4 specifically -- and nvfp4 clears the validator, so a bare rc==96 is equally consistent with a rejected declaration, an argument-parser error and a real refusal. Each arm is therefore scored on WHICH channel spoke. The deciding arm exits 96 from the loop's own refusal site naming the absent backend, trains nothing, writes ZERO checkpoint artifacts and records stage=refused with precision=nvfp4, satisfying this row's declared control arm in full. The same fixtures at bf16 exit 0, train to completion, write 7 checkpoint artifacts and record an observed dtype histogram of 338 BF16 tensors against the declaration -- so the absence of weights beside the refusal is a measured emptiness, not an untested one. A third arm shows the refusal fires even when the model cannot resolve, and a fourth shows that an unresolvable model is otherwise fatal (exit 5), which is what makes the third evidence of ordering rather than indifference. Unlike the declared video and audio rows, the declaration surface here reaches the refusal that exists.

rows.claim: reloaded weights are bit-identical (save->load parity)
rows.control_arm: perturb one tensor -> parity must go RED
rows.status: MEASURED and GREEN on a GB200 tray, with a control that could have fired and did. History: this row read "verify/parity.py SHIPPED, no run", and that was literally true -- src/foundationscale/verify/parity.py is a 1053-line library with no argparse, no main and no __main__ block, so nothing outside the unit tests had ever pointed it at a checkpoint that the framework itself wrote. A shipped comparator that has never compared a real artifact is a declaration, not a measurement. The row now carries an adjudicator, t1_4_save_load_parity.py, which runs two arms over a real on-disk safetensors checkpoint and decides from the compared counts alone. The identity arm is a genuine round trip and not a self-comparison: it copies the checkpoint, loads and re-SAVES every shard through safetensors with its metadata, and compares that against the ORIGINAL bytes. Comparing a checkpoint against itself would ask only whether one file reads the same way twice, which is very nearly a tautology, whereas the row claims save then load, so the arm has to write. The control is exactly one element of exactly one tensor stepped by +1 ULP, the smallest nonzero perturbation the dtype can represent, chosen because anything larger cannot distinguish an exact comparator from a merely tight one -- a detector that only notices a big change would pass this row while being blind to the corruption it exists to catch. Both arms are materialised by the same re-save routine, so the single perturbed element is the ONLY difference between them and a divergence in their verdicts is attributable to it and to nothing else; without that symmetry the perturbed arm would be the only one carrying re-save artifacts, and a dtype or metadata change on write would be scored as the control firing when the control had in fact not been tested. The tolerance policy is strict by construction: max_abs_diff 0, cosine at least 1.0, relative Frobenius 0. Measured against the adapter checkpoint that the T1-21 image arm saved through the framework's own save path, the identity arm compared 98 keys and 1,511,424 elements and came back ok, and the perturbed arm compared the SAME 98 keys and the SAME 1,511,424 elements and came back not ok, catching the step at element 0 of base_model.model.model.language_model.layers.0.self_attn.q_proj.lora_A.weight where 0.004369848873466253 became 0.004369849339127541 -- a last-bit change in fp32. So the comparator is exact and it is not blind, which are two separate claims and both are needed. The verdict order is load-bearing and refuses before it judges: 96 if the two arms did not compare the same key set, because that is two instruments rather than one instrument twice; 96 if the identity arm compared ZERO elements, because an empty comparison is the all-of-an-empty-set shape and is never a pass; 95 if no perturbable tensor exists at all, because a control that could not be applied is an absence and not a failure; only then 5 for a round trip that changed bits, 5 for a control that did not fire, and 0. The self-test drives that pure verdict function over synthetic payloads with no GPU, no model, no network and no filesystem, and passes 8 of 8 controls, including a MUST-FIRE for both RED branches, both 96 branches and the 95 branch, plus two controls that pin the ORDER so a key-set mismatch cannot be reported as a bit difference. Honest limitation, stated rather than buried: this is measured at adapter scale, 98 tensors and 1.51M elements, not at full-model scale. The comparator is the same code path at any size, but the row does not yet carry a reading over a 7.94B-parameter checkpoint, and re-saving one of those twice is tens of GB of estate I/O that has not been spent.

rows.claim: DCP<->HF parity VERIFICATION: the framework can read a DCP checkpoint and a safetensors checkpoint through one interface and adjudicate truthfully whether they agree. The word 'converted' has been dropped from the original claim because no DCP->HF converter exists in this source; the verifier does, and only the verifier is claimed

rows.control_arm: four controls, not the one originally declared: one element moved by a single ULP (must be seen and graded CLOSE, not absorbed), the same element moved past the tolerance (must block and name the key, which is what makes the tolerance a ceiling rather than a rubber stamp), one tensor dropped (must fail as a one-sided key, a distinct mode from a numeric finding), and disjoint key sets (must be vacuous, never ok)
rows.cost: ~40 s measured, CPU only, no GPU and no download (the ~20 min estimate was wrong)
rows.status: MEASURED GREEN (#485) on parity VERIFICATION, and it RETRACTS what this row used to say. The row read 'ABSENT', inferred from reading the source rather than from a run, and that is the third such inference this week to be withdrawn by measurement (after T1-18 and T1-19). The subject is not synthesised: the HF side is the safetensors checkpoint the training plane actually wrote during T1-19. The DCP side is written by torch's own writer, because this plane never emits DCP -- it refuses sharded execution (T1-14) -- and that asymmetry is the point, since the question is whether FoundationScale can read BOTH and tell the truth. It can. Identical inputs: 26 keys, 19743872 elements, every key graded bitwise-EXACT. One element moved by a single bf16 ULP: SEEN -- exactly one mismatched element, max absolute difference 0.0001220703125 -- and graded CLOSE, not EXACT, against the declared policy default-close (max_abs_diff<=0.01, cosine>=0.999, rel_frob<=0.01). That grade is the load-bearing detail: ok means 'within the declared tolerance', not 'identical', and because the grade is three-level rather than boolean, ok never hides a bitwise difference from a reader who looks. The same element moved by 1.0: graded DIFFER, blocks, names the key, so the tolerance is a ceiling that demonstrably can be exceeded rather than a policy that acquits everything. One tensor dropped: reported as a one-sided key, not as a numeric finding. Every key renamed: VACUOUS and not ok, so the all([]) guard this framework exists to hunt is live in the framework's own comparator rather than merely documented there. Adjudicated by t1_7_dcp_hf_parity_arms.py, 24 self-test controls, CLEAR on both the cluster's 3.11 interpreter and the laptop's 3.14. NOT established here: that FoundationScale can CONVERT between the formats -- it cannot, and the claim above was narrowed rather than left to be read as if it could; nor parity across a SHARDED DCP checkpoint with multiple write ranks, which no instrument can reach while the plane refuses sharded execution.

rows.claim: an MoE model trains and experts receive gradient
rows.control_arm: a router that never routes = zero grad on some experts; must be detected
rows.status: RUNTIME ARM RUN, and the defect that blocked adjudication is now FIXED and re-measured; the row is still not green and the reason for that has changed. MEASURED on a GB200 tray: a real 26B-A4B MoE (128 experts over 30 layers) trains end-to-end through the shipped CLI -- LoRA rank 8 on thirty language layers, ag_news, 10 steps, rc 0, checkpoint written and the save gates ran. So "an MoE model trains" is established. When this row was first written the second half could not be adjudicated at all, because the framework declared the model DENSE and both expert gates skipped as "0 units (dense model)" on a model with 128 of them. That is #471, and #498 is its root cause: the config reader was a flat top-level getattr while every MoE on this estate nests the count under text_config (Gemma4Config 128; Qwen3_5MoeConfig 256 on both 35B-A3B checkpoints, so it is the transformers 5.x convention and not a multimodal quirk). Both are fixed. Re-MEASURED against the artifacts this arm itself produced, reading the safetensors header only: the flat read returns None where the tree read returns text_config.num_experts=128; the declaration is now UNKNOWN -- config declares 128 experts but 0 of 110 tensors are expert-named, the two sources disagree, so neither is adopted -- and both expert gates return a named abstention, "adapter-only checkpoint: all 110 of 110 saved tensor name(s) are adapter-namespaced", which states in words that it is NOT a claim the model is dense. The earlier note that searching text_config first sends every LoRA run over an MoE to a false RED no longer describes the behaviour: that false RED WAS the missing adapter-scope abstention, which is now implemented and carries a control proving a GUTTED checkpoint still blocks. What remains is a limit of the arm, not a defect: under LoRA the expert weights are never in the artifact, so "experts receive gradient" cannot be established here in principle and the honest verdict is the abstention. Establishing it needs a full-weight MoE arm, which is a different and far more expensive run. The control arm (a router that never routes) is still unrun, and is no longer blocked. Also measured on the way in: the bare suffix q_proj reaches the VISION tower on this family, where it is a Gemma4ClippableLinear that peft refuses, so the first attempt died before step 1 and adapter targets must be spelled language-scoped. #499 is open on the same code path and is published as open: train/loop.py reads five expert-count key names while the provenance producer and the probe read three, so a model declaring one of the two extra names would be MoE to the trainer and dense to the record. No model measured here uses those names; it is pinned by controls that freeze both lists, and unifying them would invalidate rows measured against the narrow list. CONTROL ARM RUN, AND IT FOUND ITS OWN INSTRUMENT MISSING (#500). The declared control -- a router that never routes, so some experts take zero gradient -- was executed for the first time as a mechanism study on a tiny FULL-WEIGHT Qwen2-MoE (4 experts, 2 MoE layers, 181,440 parameters, 30 AdamW steps), the two arms differing ONLY by a forward hook that masks experts 2 and 3 out of the router's top-k; seed, init, data, optimiser and step count are identical, so any difference is attributable to routing alone. The hook does what it claims: the step-0 per-expert max absolute gradient in the control arm is e0=4.252e-03, e1=2.916e-03, e2=0.000e+00, e3=0.000e+00, against e2=2.167e-03 in the run arm. But at the AdamW DEFAULT weight_decay=0.01 the zero-gradient experts still MOVED, by 2.166e-04 and 2.294e-04 against 2.19e-01 for the routed ones, and the count of bitwise-frozen experts was zero -- so an exact-equality movement probe reports a never-routed expert as trained. Re-run at weight_decay=0.0 the same two experts are bitwise EXACT at 0.000e+00 and the frozen set is exactly (2, 3), which is the control proving decoupled weight decay is the cause: AdamW decays every parameter whether or not it has a gradient. The separation is still about 1000x in magnitude, so a THRESHOLD instrument works and an exact-equality one does not. Second half, and the reason this row cannot simply adopt the shipped parity instrument: parity is keyed per FQN, and the dominant HF MoE layout stacks every expert of a layer into ONE tensor (`model.layers.0.mlp.experts.gate_up_proj`, shape (4, 128, 64)), so parity returns DIFFER for BOTH arms identically and cannot see the dead expert at any weight-decay setting. That is ExpertDistinctnessGate's own documented stacked-layout blind spot, now measured at the data level as well as the metadata level. So the control arm is no longer unrun: it ran, it is reproducible, and it establishes that no shipped FoundationScale instrument detects the condition this row says must be detected. What the row still needs is a full-weight MoE driven through the shipped entry point plus a per-expert-slice, threshold-based probe; #500 is published open rather than fixed on release eve, because adding an instrument is a new claim and this row has no budget left to measure one. STAGE C RUN THROUGH THE SHIPPED ENTRY POINT, AND IT CORRECTS TWO SENTENCES OF #500 (#501). The follow-up #500 said this row still needed -- a full-weight MoE driven through the shipped entry point plus a per-expert-slice probe -- has now been run. Fixture: a REAL-architecture Gemma4 MoE, every structural knob inherited from the estate's shipped gemma-4-26B-A4B config (the same Gemma4TextConfig class, the same Gemma4TextRouter, enable_moe_block=true, the same stacked expert layout) and only the sizes shrunk, to 2 layers, 8 experts, top-k 2, 70,198,672 parameters. Both arms are `python -m foundationscale.train.cli` on ag_news, full-weight, 30 steps, seed 42, precision bf16 declared, byte-identical command lines; the ONLY difference is an environment variable read by a shim that writes -inf into the router's own expert_scores before its softmax, so experts 2 and 3 are never routed. POSITIVE CONTROL: in the run arm experts 2 and 3 received 936 and 771 routed tokens; in the control arm they received 0 and 0, and the other six absorbed the traffic. FIRST CORRECTION TO #500: #500 recorded that decoupled weight decay moves a zero-gradient expert and defeats an exact-equality probe. That holds for the hand-rolled torch.optim.AdamW #500 used, whose default weight_decay is 0.01. It does NOT apply to this framework's own path: FoundationScale never sets weight decay and inherits transformers TrainingArguments, so the arms above ran at weight_decay=0.0 under adamw_torch_fused, read back from the saved training_args. On the shipped path an exact-equality movement probe is therefore sound, and #500's warning should be read as scoped to an optimiser FoundationScale does not construct. RESULT OF THE PER-SLICE PROBE: in the control arm all four stacked expert tensors give exactly 0.000e+00 movement at slices 2 and 3 and the bitwise-frozen set is exactly (2, 3), while the six live experts move by about 6e-04, which is the bf16 resolution at that magnitude; in the run arm no slice is frozen at all, so the probe does not false-positive. The remedy #500 proposed works, and on this path it needs no threshold. WHAT PARITY SEES: the shipped per-FQN comparator returns DIFFER for all four stacked tensors in BOTH arms identically, so #500's second half is confirmed on a real architecture through the real entry point rather than only on a toy. SECOND AND MORE IMPORTANT CORRECTION TO #500: #500 concluded that nothing FoundationScale ships detects the condition this row says must be detected. Nothing detects it, but that sentence understates the framework and is withdrawn as written. Run against these checkpoints, the shipped checkpoint.expert_distinctness gate does not pass and does not stay silent: it returns SKIP with abstention NOT_ESTABLISHED, names the stacked layout, reports that all four leading dims equal the declared 8 experts and that every metadata property it CAN check was checked and showed nothing wrong, states that per-expert identity inside a stacked tensor is unobservable from metadata by construction, and names the remedy in its own words -- a data-level per-slice comparison that hashes every expert slice within each stacked tensor, which is precisely the probe run above. Because NOT_ESTABLISHED stays inside the denominator, checkpoint.first_save then reports UNDERCOVERED at 2 of 3 sub-gates and stops the run, rc 5, in both arms. So the honest statement is that FoundationScale cannot see a never-routed expert and refuses to certify the checkpoint instead of passing it, which is the doctrine working rather than failing. NEGATIVE RESULT worth recording so the cheap shortcut is not attempted: router.per_expert_scale is the one genuinely per-expert-indexed 1-D tensor in this architecture, and it is bitwise frozen for ALL EIGHT experts in BOTH arms, as is router.scale, so it carries no signal and cannot serve as a dead-expert detector. SCALE CHECK on the real artifact rather than the fixture: the shipped gemma-4-26B-A4B stacks 128 experts per layer over 30 layers, so 3,840 expert MLPs sit behind 60 per-FQN keys, and the same probe run there resolved num_experts=128 from text_config with the artifact census corroborating, against 0 for its dense 31B sibling. #501 is filed, not fixed: the per-slice hash is now measured and prescribed by the gate itself, but adding it as a shipped instrument is a new claim.

rows.claim: an image-bearing corpus trains and the vision tower's weights MOVE
rows.control_arm: a text-only arm through the same path: tower weights must NOT move
rows.status: MEASURED and GREEN on a GB200 tray, with a control that could have fired and did not. History: the declared-image arm was PROCESSOR-FAMILY DEPENDENT and unreachable on Gemma-4 for three independent causes (#448, follow-up to #371) -- a flat image list that normalises to ONE image-batch so N images and N texts read as 1 vs N, raw row text carrying no chat template and so no placeholder token for the pixels to land on, and a constant TOKENIZE_MAX_LENGTH smaller than the prompt surface's OWN recorded tokens per image. #449 fixed the shape on BOTH planes that write it -- the train collator and the RL rollout encode path -- by nesting one image sub-list per feature, including an EMPTY sub-list for a text-only row, and by building text through the processor's OWN apply_chat_template so no family's placeholder is hardcoded. #450 then fixed the objective that a GREEN run had hidden: labels were input_ids.clone(), and MEASURED over four corpus rows 73.6 percent of label positions were the image placeholder id, whose input embedding is replaced by vision-encoder output, so emitting it as text is never a valid target. That run reported train_loss 19.16 against ln(vocab) 12.477, worse than uniform random; masking placeholders and padding took the identical command to 3.845. Both families now collate through the SHIPPED code with zero placeholders and zero pad slots left unmasked and a non-vacuous supervised count: gemma-4-E4B-it resolves placeholder id 258880, qwen2.5-vl-32b resolves 151655 from a PROCESSOR-ONLY attribute that a tokenizer-first order returns None for. The row's own claim is now measured directly rather than deferred. A full fine-tune cannot watch the tower move here, 7.94B parameters of weights plus fp32 Adam state against roughly 35 GiB of free device memory, so the arms use LoRA as an exact instrument: lora_B is zero-initialised and AdamW skips a parameter whose grad is None, so a nonzero norm is movement with no tolerance to argue about. Both arms attach the SAME adapter to the SAME 49 modules -- 48 matched by suffixes that exist only inside the vision tower, plus ONE language module that is not under test and is the control's control, because a text-only arm whose vision LoRA is still zero proves nothing if that arm never trained at all. Ten steps each on gemma-4-E4B-it, gradient checkpointing OFF because pixel values never require grad and a checkpointed vision segment can silently yield none, both arms rc 0: the image arm moved 48 of 48 vision-tower modules at a worst absolute B norm of 1.7055e-02, and the text-only arm, the same rows with the image column stripped, moved 0 of 48 while still moving its language anchor 1 of 1. So the control arm demonstrably trained and the tower still did not move. Run three times -- twice ad hoc and once through the shipped adjudicator on bytes md5-matched to the committed blob. The 48-of-48 against 0-of-48 split is identical every time because it is a bit-exact question; the worst norm moves in the third decimal (1.7105e-02, 1.7084e-02, 1.7055e-02) because lora_A is randomly initialised per run, which is also how one can tell the number was re-measured rather than re-read. The row now carries an adjudicator rather than prose: t1_21_vision_tower_arms.py runs both arms, classifies each adapted module by the same suffix rule peft used to select it, and decides from the norms alone. Its --self-test needs no GPU, no model and no network and drives the real adjudication function over synthetic norms -- 15 of 15 controls PASS, with a MUST-FIRE control behind every RED, 95 and 96 branch, including the one that matters most: an unmoved tower in a control arm that moved NOTHING AT ALL is reported 95, never GREEN, because that arm never trained. Found en route and fixed as a precondition (#451): the train CLI's only repeatable flag, --adapter-target, raised AttributeError inside argparse on EVERY use, because the declared-fields probe rewrites every default to a sentinel object and argparse's append action calls .append on a copy of it, so the flag could not be used at all.
